description: Identifiers a caller says out loud, for the spelled-identifier robustness suite. Each case is one string the agent has to end up holding exactly, because an identifier is a database key and a near miss returns nothing rather than something worse.
design_notes: SEEDED FROM A REAL FAILURE. `name_yusuf_rossi` is the exact identifier that failed in the published half-duplex retail run (results/whissle/HD_RETAIL_2026-08-06.md): the agent called find_user_id_by_name_zip with first_name Youssef against a customer whose record reads yusuf_rossi_9620, and the lookup returned nothing. The postcode in that same call was heard correctly. The name alone was enough to lose the task, so it is case one.

NAMES ARE OVER-REPRESENTED ON PURPOSE. The published voice run used a single simulated customer, so its name failure is one sample repeated rather than several independent ones — a limitation the benchmark page states about itself. The corpus answers that directly with distinct names across several orthographic traditions, since a recogniser tuned on one distribution fails unevenly across them and a single Anglo name would never show it.

HOMOPHONE PAIRS ARE INCLUDED AS SEPARATE CASES so the suite can distinguish 'the recogniser cannot hear this class of sound' from 'the recogniser picked the wrong member of a pair it heard fine'. Those have different fixes: one is acoustic, the other wants a constrained vocabulary or a readback.

ALPHANUMERIC CASES USE CONFUSABLE CHARACTERS deliberately — B/P/D/V/E, M/N, S/F, 5/9, 0/O. An order-id benchmark made of unambiguous characters would report a healthy number and predict nothing about production.

`spoken_as` is what the simulated caller is instructed to say. It is not a second ground truth: the agent is scored against `truth` only, so a case where the caller spells it out and a case where the caller says it naturally are different difficulties of the same target.

cases.spoken_as: say your name naturally, do not spell it unless asked
cases.note: The exact failure from the published voice retail run. Heard as 'Youssef Rossi'; the lookup returned no customer and the task was lost.

cases.spoken_as: say your name naturally; spell the first name only if asked
cases.note: Orthography and pronunciation diverge sharply. A recogniser that has not seen the spelling will not reconstruct it from the sound.

cases.spoken_as: say your full name naturally
cases.note: Three short syllables with no redundancy — nothing for a language model to recover a mis-heard token from.

cases.spoken_as: say your name, then spell the first name
cases.note: Consonant cluster plus a spell-out. Tests the spelling path, not just the name path.

cases.spoken_as: say your name naturally
cases.note: Hyphenated surname: normalisation must not let 'Al Rashid' and 'Al-Rashid' diverge, while keeping 'Al-Rasheed' a genuine miss.

cases.spoken_as: say your name naturally
cases.note: Half of a homophone pair with `name_homophone_sara_alt`. Same sound, different key.

cases.spoken_as: say your name naturally
cases.note: The other half. If both cases pass, the agent is not guessing from a prior.

cases.spoken_as: read the order number out character by character
cases.note: B/P/D are the classic confusable set; 9 sits next to 5 acoustically.

cases.spoken_as: read the order number out character by character
cases.note: M/N, plus a leading zero that is routinely dropped.

cases.spoken_as: read the order number naturally, at your own pace
cases.note: The same task without a spell-out instruction. The delta against the spelled cases is the value of asking callers to spell.

cases.spoken_as: read it in groups, as it is printed
cases.note: Repeated digits: 'double eight' and 'eight eight' must both land on 88.

cases.spoken_as: read the postcode digit by digit
cases.note: The postcode from the published failing run. It was heard correctly there — kept as a control, so a regression on the easy case is visible.

cases.spoken_as: read the postcode as you would to a courier
cases.note: Mixed letters and digits with an internal space that carries no information.

cases.spoken_as: read the postal code character by character
cases.note: Alternating letters and digits, with 0/O adjacent.

cases.spoken_as: give your email address; say 'dot' and 'at' where they appear
cases.note: Spoken punctuation must normalise; the local part must not.

cases.spoken_as: give your email address, spelling the part before the at sign
cases.note: Underscore, digits and a two-part suffix in one string.

cases.spoken_as: give your phone number as you would say it out loud
cases.note: Separators are formatting; the country code is not. Normalisation keeps the plus and drops the rest.

cases.spoken_as: give your phone number, in pairs
cases.note: Indian numbers are commonly read in pairs, which is where digit-pair mishearing shows up.

cases.spoken_as: read the case reference exactly as printed
cases.note: Mixed case plus hyphens plus a leading-zero run.

cases.spoken_as: read the reference using the phonetic alphabet if you know it
cases.note: Tests whether a phonetic-alphabet read-out helps or hurts. Nobody has measured which.
